How to Play Multiversal – Quick Overview
Multiversal is a collaborative roleplaying game where players create characters, explore vast realities, 
and shape the multiverse through their actions. The Game Master (GM) presents the world and 
challenges, while players control their characters, making decisions that impact the unfolding story.
🎭  Roles in the Game
✔  Game Master (GM): Acts as the worldʼs narrator, referee, and facilitator. The GM sets up scenarios, 
roleplays NPCs, and adjudicates rules while allowing player actions to shape the story.
✔  Players: Control unique characters with their own skills, knowledge, and abilities. They explore, 
interact, and take on challenges, using dice rolls to determine outcomes.
🎲  Core Gameplay Mechanics
Rolling Dice to Determine Outcomes
Multiversal uses a D20-based system (20-sided dice) for resolving actions and challenges.
•Basic Roll: Roll 1d20 + relevant skill/ability modifier.
•Success or Failure: The GM sets a Difficulty Check (DC) (e.g., DC 15).
◦ If you meet or exceed the DC, you succeed.
◦ If you roll below the DC, you fail.
•Opposed Rolls: When competing (e.g., sneaking vs. an NPCʼs perception), both sides roll, and the 
higher result wins.
📌  Example: If you try to hack a secure terminal (DC 18) and roll 14 + Hacking skill (5) = 19, you 
succeed.

to think carefully about where they travel and how long they linger.

•The ruins of civilization should be eerie and unsettling. Descriptions of decayed landmarks, 
strange noises, and faded remnants of life add atmosphere.

abilities, while others impose significant drawbacks. Let players choose whether to embrace or

📺  Toon Creature Type
Introduction: What Is a Toon?
Toons are creatures native to the Unreal Zone—an unstable, absurd branch of the multiverse where logic bends, 
physics performs slapstick, and reality is a suggestion at best. Toons operate not by biology or machinery, but by 
principles of exaggeration, intent, and narrative momentum. They are not a species but a creature type, unified 
by their shared defiance of consistent physical laws.
A toon might resemble a person, animal, object, or abstract idea given shape. Their internal makeup could be ink, 
chalk, static, performance energy, or unknown materials that only exist under toon physics. They are often 
animated by emotion, attention, and genre rules rather than anatomy or energy.
While many toons are native to the Unreal Zone, others emerge through toonification—a process by which 
prolonged exposure to toon logic alters the body and mind. Some beings may even become toons unintentionally 
after violating too many causal principles or falling into recursive narrative loops.
🎭  Core Traits of Toon Creatures
All creatures with the Toon type share the following traits, regardless of subtype or appearance:
🌀  Toon Body
Toons do not have organs, bones, or standard physiology. Instead, they are composed of toon matter such as ink, 
joke-logic, or ambient narrative energy.
•Immune to fall damage, suffocation, non-magical diseases, and poisons.
•Resistance to bludgeoning and slashing unless the damage is narratively appropriate (e.g., giant comedic 
mallet, serious dramatic strike).
📣  Stretch & Squash
As a free action, toons can compress, stretch, inflate, or reshape their bodies for effect. This includes:
•Passing through tight spaces regardless of size.
•Bouncing back from crushing or flattening effects.
•Exaggerating features for comedic or dramatic purposes.
This is not shapeshifting—identity remains intact. It's physical comedy with mechanical relevance.
🎬  Toon Save
Once per short or long rest, a toon can reroll any failed attack, save, or check if the reroll results in a funnier, 
more fitting, or narratively satisfying outcome. This must be approved by the GM and reflect the sceneʼs tone.
🧲  Genre Magnetism
Toons subtly distort nearby reality to match their internal tone. When a toon is active in a scene, the GM may:
•Alter flavor and tone of local reality (e.g., a noir toon darkens the lighting and adds rain).

🌿  Plant-Based Creatures in Multiversal
Plant-based creatures exist across the infinite multiverse, from primeval forests and arcane gardens to 
corrupted void jungles and hyper-evolved biotech biomes. Unlike typical fauna, plant creatures often 
interact with the environment in unique ways—rooting into terrain, spreading through spores or roots, 
and responding to stimuli with slow but overwhelming intent. Their motivations are not always predatory 
or sapient; many simply act in accordance with alien growth instincts or ancient programming.
Some plant creatures are wild and natural; others are the product of magical tampering, divine 
intervention, artificial cultivation, or mutation by multiversal energies. They can serve as hazards, allies, 
sources of rare resources, or entire ecosystems unto themselves.
📖  Mechanical Traits of Plant Creatures
All creatures with the Plant tag share the following baseline mechanics unless otherwise noted:
•Immunity to Charm and Sleep: Plant creatures cannot be charmed or magically put to sleep unless 
they possess a defined nervous system or mind structure.
•Resistance to Poison: Most plant creatures have resistance to poison damage and advantage on 
saving throws against the Poisoned condition.
•Vulnerabilities: Many plant creatures are vulnerable to fire damage unless they come from fire-
adapted ecosystems.
•Photosensitive or Energy-Dependent: Some plants require environmental conditions (sunlight, 
heat, mana, etc.) to maintain full functionality. In low-energy environments, they may act sluggish or 
lose traits.
•Harvestable Traits: Defeating or interacting with plant creatures may yield alchemical, magical, or 
nutritional materials (GM's discretion or per stat block).
•Root Sense (Optional): Many immobile or creeping plant creatures can sense vibrations in a 30–60 
ft radius through the ground, functioning similarly to Tremorsense but not working on solid metal, 
air, or void.
•Regrowth (Optional): Some plant creatures may regrow or reanimate after death if not fully 
destroyed (burned, uprooted, or disenchanted).

Reading the Current
•Fate Tarot, bone casting, or divine communions.
•Reality Mapping Devices that detect narrative density.
•Travelerʼs Instinct (passive trait that alerts characters to potential anchors or divergence points).
•Dream Echoes (hallucinations, deja vu, visions from other timelines).

with a split in three directions.”
Fate Reading Check
1d20 + Wisdom or Intelligence + relevant skill/tool bonus
On success, the player learns:
•The next likely anchor event
•How difficult it will be to resist the current
•The presence of unseen fateweavers or counterforces
Course Correction
If players wish to deviate from the current:
•They must spend Sanity, XP, or use a Narrative Interference Mechanism (see below).
•Failure causes backlash: reality strain, paradox surge, or echo bleed.
7.3 Fate Anchors and Probability Artifacts
Some items or beings are infused with fate—they either guide a current or resist it.
Fate Anchors:
•Individuals or objects that must exist or fulfill a role in every possible version of a reality.
•Cannot be easily killed, changed, or removed.
•Interacting with them without syncing may cause timeline warps or memory overlap.

󰍽  Specificity (How Clear is Your Intent?)
🔹  Low Specificity →  Vague or open-ended wording.

🔹  High Specificity →  A very precise and complex request.

Procedure: Converting a Monster into a Playable Species
1.Choose the Base Version (Lowest CR)
•Select the lowest CR version of the creature available in the manual.
•Keep all natural attacks, movement modes, and base physical characteristics from this version.
2.Determine Playable Traits
•Keep any physical traits that are inherent to the species, such as: 
◦ Size
◦ Speed (land, flight, swim, burrow)
◦ Natural armor (if applicable)
◦ Darkvision, echolocation, etc.
◦ Natural weapons (claws, bite, etc.)
3.Assign Base XP Cost for the Species
•Base XP cost is determined by the original creatureʼs CR × 500 XP.
•If the creature has abilities requiring resources (e.g., spell slots, limited uses per day), discount 
the cost by 25% to account for their limited usability.
4.List Abilities as Unlockable Powers
•All unique abilities (such as breath weapons, magic resistance, or special movement mechanics) 
are locked at character creation.
•Each ability is assigned an XP cost based on its impact on gameplay.
•The player can purchase these abilities at character creation if they have the XP, or they can buy 
them later while advancing their character.
5.Adjust HP & Defenses for Balance
•The creatureʼs HP is recalculated using standard character rules (Constitution-based instead of 
monster hit dice).

◦ Immunities are not allowed at level 1, but can be bought later.

🐾  Introduction to Animal Handling
In the boundless expanse of the Multiversal setting, intelligent life is not limited to bipedal species alone. Across 
countless worlds, creatures of tooth, talon, fur, feather, scale, and soul coexist with adventurers—sometimes as 
companions, sometimes as threats, and often as powerful allies.
Animal Handling in Multiversal represents a unique and versatile gameplay pillar that combines care, training, 
bonding, and specialization. Whether taming a wild beast from the bio-chasms of Cytherios, breeding 
shadowhounds in your base kennel, or guiding a dragon across hostile skies, animal handling allows characters 
to deepen their connection to the natural (and unnatural) worlds around them.
This system supports:
•🐶  Pet companions and familiars
•🐴  Mounts and exotic steeds
•🐉  Combat beasts and magical creatures
•🧬  Breeding and genetic progression
•🎖  Trained service animals and tactical support creatures
📚  Key Features
•Creature Intelligence Tiers: Whether training a loyal canine (INT 2) or tutoring a spellcasting phoenix (INT 
10), rules scale by intellect and behavior complexity.
•Training Actions: From simple commands to complex magical tasks, each behavior has a difficulty level, time 
cost, and required bond.
•Temperament System: Animals have unique personalities—affectionate, territorial, nervous, stubborn—
which directly affect handling and training.
•Breeding & Genetics: Players can engage in crossbreeding, genetic trait inheritance, and trait optimization, 
all while managing risks like mutation or inbreeding.
•Care & Maintenance: Feeding, healing, grooming, and emotional health all impact long-term performance 
and loyalty.
•Market, Trade & Prestige: Animals can be raised, sold, shown in competition, or registered as multiversal 
breeds for wealth and fame.
•Advanced Customization: For those with the right skills, creatures may even be trained in stealth, magical 
rituals, or battlefield strategy.
Whether youʼre a gentle beast whisperer, a merciless warbeast master, or a scientific breeder with a geneforge, 
Animal Handling gives you powerful, enduring allies and narrative tools.
🧬  Types of Creatures & Classification
In Multiversal, animals and trainable creatures span the spectrum from mundane beasts to sentient magical or 
technological life. To manage this diversity in gameplay, creatures are grouped by Category, Size, Intelligence 
Tier, and Temperament Profile. These classifications help determine training complexity, bonding potential, and 
compatibility with specific commands or breeding systems.

In a culture that spans the multiverse, religion would evolve in highly diverse, syncretic, and 
philosophical ways due to the vast array of experiences, existential dilemmas, and encounters with the 
divine, supernatural, and cosmic unknown. Here are some possible religious movements and why they

Why It Develops:
A civilization that moves between realities would eventually begin to question the idea of a singular, 
static deity. Instead, many might adopt a belief in an infinite or fractal divinity—an entity that exists in all 
forms, in all realities, simultaneously.
Core Beliefs:
•The "Fractal Divinity" is neither one god nor many, but an ever-repeating and self-reflecting pattern 
of consciousness spread across all dimensions.
•Worship is focused on understanding and interpreting glimpses of this pattern, which appear in 
different forms across realities.
•Followers practice sacred geometry, probability manipulation, and deep meditation to attune 
themselves to the multiverseʼs hidden rhythms.

•Others revere them but see their departure as a cosmic test—followers must continue the act of

4. Culture and Society
Elves are known for their sophisticated and artistic societies, valuing harmony, beauty, magic, and the 
pursuit of knowledge. While elven societies vary greatly across different realities, the Elarian Elves of 
Heimenhearthʼs multiverse are the most influential. As stewards of the Etherflotilla—a cosmic fleet of 
living ships created after their original planet, Elaria, was mined by dwarves—they travel across 
realities, maintaining the flora, fauna, and remnants of their homeworld. The Etherflotilla serves as both 
their sanctuary and a center for multiversal exploration, making them ambassadors, explorers, and 
diplomats across realms.
Elarian Elves maintain complex social structures, with each flotilla vessel often governed by a council of 
elders, representing noble houses, guilds, and arcane institutions. They are masters of the arcane arts, 
shaping their environment and using Orilaunʼs magic to create architectural marvels, artwork, and 
magical artifacts. Each Elarian Elf sees themselves as a protector of their heritage and the magic of 
Elaria, whether through diplomacy, arcane study, or stewardship of the Etherflotillaʼs natural sanctuaries.
---

1. Introduction to Multiversal Dynamics
“Youʼre not in one world. Youʼre in all of them. Some just havenʼt noticed you yet.” — Traveler Saying
1.1 What It Means to Traverse the Multiverse
Operating in the multiverse isnʼt just about hopping from world to world—itʼs about existing in an environment 
where possibility itself is tangible, layered, and ever-shifting. In Multiversal, adventurers are more than 
wanderers; they are quantum actors in an interconnected, fluid lattice of timelines, worlds, and branches. Every 
decision, every movement, and every interaction is potentially reflected in alternate forms across realities—
sometimes subtly, sometimes catastrophically.
Multiversal dynamics refer to the unique physics, metaphysics, and narrative implications of such a structure. 
They encompass:
•Parallel realities and alternate timelines
•Encountering or merging with versions of yourself
•Navigating shifting fate currents
•Traveling with others while desynced in reality
•Moving between branches and resisting multiversal strain
Unlike single-world campaigns, multiversal adventures demand a different kind of awareness. Every world has its 
own "rules," and some rules break when you're not from there. Syncing to a reality can grant power, while 
resisting its pull may protect your identity—or shred it.
1.2 Key Concepts and Foundations
To help players and GMs alike grasp multiversal dynamics, this section will introduce the following foundational 
ideas:
•Reality vs Timeline – A reality is a world with its own laws and traits. A timeline is a linear sequence of events 
within a reality or set of realities. Timelines can branch, collapse, or merge.
•Branch – A large-scale grouping of similar realities, often defined by shared metaphysical laws or origin 
points. For example, the Mortalitas branch contains death-aligned worlds.
•Sync State – A measure of how in-phase a character is with the current reality. Being out-of-sync can cause 
dissonance, rejection, or even hallucinations.
•Echo Selves – Alternate versions of a character that exist in other timelines or realities. Sometimes helpful. 
Sometimes unhinged. Sometimes already dead.
•Fate Currents – Invisible narrative flows that tug at characters, pushing or pulling them toward likely 
outcomes unless resisted or redirected.
